units.function: name the three stages of the argument in the order the reader will meet them

original_instantiations: The argument runs as such: a first look gives the lay of the land, a simulation then checks the hunch, and a differential model offers a quicker theoretical stand-in.
The write-up runs as such: a sketch, then a simulation that checks it, then a differential stand-in for a faster look.

units.source_excerpt: This model progresses as such: the preliminary analysis serves to give an overview of the problem. Next, the agent-based model and the accompanying simulations then validate our ideas. Then, the differential equation model gives a theoretical approach that may be more amenable to quick analysis.
units.reusable_pattern: [The argument] runs as such: [first pass] gives an overview. Next, [the check]. Then, [a faster stand-in].
reusable_elements: occurrences: summary sheet, second paragraph.
stable function: tell the reader the order of models before any equation appears.
pattern: progresses as such / Next / Then.
slots: overview model, validating simulation, fast theoretical approximator.
boundary: three stages only; do not stretch the cadence past the models the paper actually runs.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not turn this into a claim that every paper should stack three models.
Do not copy the Louvre or exit-sign wording.

units.function: label the opening strategy as a guess rather than a proven optimum

original_instantiations: We start from a routing rule that simply sends each person to the nearest door, treated as a first guess at the plan that clears the hall fastest.
We begin with a rule that points everyone to the nearest door, and we treat that as a first guess, not a proven best.

units.source_excerpt: We start with an evacuation strategy where exit signs simply point to the nearest exit as a heuristic guess for the best plan to minimize evacuation time.
units.reusable_pattern: We start with [a simple rule] as a heuristic guess for [the quantity we want to minimize].
information_order: the quantity it is guessing at
reusable_elements: occurrences: summary sheet, third paragraph.
stable function: keep a baseline from being read as an optimum.
pattern: simply X as a heuristic guess for Y.
boundary: the guess must later be tested or replaced; do not leave it as the recommendation.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not claim nearest-exit routing is generally optimal.
Do not reuse museum or bomb wording.

units.function: open on a widely known object, then pivot to the risk that fame creates

original_instantiations: The hall is famous and it draws a crowd all year. When something goes wrong, those people have to get out, and the responders still have to get in.
It is a well-known place and it stays busy. In a crisis the visitors have to leave while the people who help them still have to arrive.

units.source_excerpt: The Louvre is a famous art museum that houses many incredible artworks, including the Mona Lisa. As a result, the Louvre attracts many tourists and enthusiasts all throughout the year. In an event of an emergency, it is crucial that people are able to evacuate effectively while also allowing emergency personnel to get to a target location.
units.reusable_pattern: [Place] is famous for [object]. As a result it draws [a crowd]. In an emergency, [they must leave] while [helpers must still arrive].
reusable_elements: occurrences: page 3, section 1, opening paragraph.
stable function: earn the modeling problem from a public fact in three sentences.
pattern: famous for X. As a result, crowd. In an emergency, leave and arrive.
boundary: the two directions of motion must both be stated or the pivot collapses.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not treat fame itself as evidence about flow.
Do not copy the named artwork.

units.function: concede that emergencies differ, then name the single thing they share

original_instantiations: Crises differ: some call for caution and some are plain. The one thing they share is a way out.
Not every emergency looks the same. The one thing they have in common is a planned way out.

units.source_excerpt: Emergencies are multi-faceted; some situations require a more cautious approach while others may be straightforward. However, the one congruity in this multi-faceted system is an exit plan.
units.reusable_pattern: [Cases] differ; some need [caution], others are [plain]. However, the one congruity is [the shared object].
reusable_elements: occurrences: page 3, section 2, first paragraph.
stable function: narrow a wide problem to one decision variable.
pattern: multi-faceted; however, the one congruity is X.
boundary: X must be the thing the rest of the paper actually models.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not use this to dismiss scenario differences that later change the answer.

units.function: justify a control device by who can read it and whether it stays on

original_instantiations: A painted arrow is a shared sign for a mixed crowd, and it keeps its own supply, so it stays readable after the lights fail.
A standard arrow is something every visitor can read, and a separate supply keeps it visible after the mains fail.

units.source_excerpt: Indeed, the arrow and universal iconography of an exit sign is a common ground for the diverse crowd of the Louvre and are usually powered by independent power sources, allowing them to stay visible even in the event of a power-outage.
units.reusable_pattern: Indeed, [the device] is a common ground for [a mixed crowd] and stays usable even when [the usual support fails].
reusable_elements: occurrences: page 3, section 2, second paragraph.
stable function: defend a low-tech control by audience and by power independence.
pattern: Indeed, X is common ground and survives Y.
boundary: both reasons are required; readability alone is not the move.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not claim signs always dominate loudspeaker or staff direction.

units.function: derive the paper's job from what a visitor cannot know

original_instantiations: If the visitors do not know the building and have no word from the authorities, they have to trust the signs. So the work is to find where the crowd jams and what to optimize.
Without local knowledge and without an official update, people fall back on the signs. That is why we look for jams and for a number we can improve.

units.source_excerpt: In the absence of information from law enforcement and potentially without a good knowledge of the locale (as in the case of tourists in the Louvre), bystanders must rely on exit signs to exit quickly. Thus, our analysis works to identify congestion, security vulnerabilities, and metrics for optimization for a robust, consistent exit plan.
units.reusable_pattern: In the absence of [official information] and without [local knowledge], [people] must rely on [the device]. Thus, our analysis works to identify [the quantities].
reusable_elements: occurrences: page 3, section 2, third paragraph.
stable function: turn an information gap into the list of things the model will measure.
pattern: in the absence of A, must rely on B. Thus we identify C.
boundary: C must be measurable in the models that follow.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not treat tourist ignorance as a general behavioral law.

units.function: warn that several everyday words name one model object

original_instantiations: A few words will be used for the same object, and they may swap places. Rooms, nodes and sites all mean one place a person can stand.
Several ordinary words name one thing in the model, and we use them interchangeably. A room, a node and a site are the same spot.

units.source_excerpt: A number of terms will be used in this paper to refer to salient feature of our model. These terms may appear interchangeably to refer to these elements.
units.reusable_pattern: A number of terms will be used for [one model object]. These terms may appear interchangeably.
reusable_elements: occurrences: page 3, section 2.1.
stable function: stop a reader treating synonyms as new variables.
pattern: terms may appear interchangeably, then a bullet of aliases.
boundary: only alias pairs the paper actually swaps; do not invent a glossary.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not collapse terms that the paper later distinguishes, such as congestion and a cut.

units.function: state how a public drawing became the graph, including what was typed by hand

original_instantiations: We marked up a public floor drawing by hand and typed in room sizes and which rooms touch, and that became the graph.
A published plan was annotated by hand, and room area and adjacency were entered manually to build the network.

units.source_excerpt: We hand annotated a publicly available floor plan, and manually entered data about room size and connectivity to create a graph.
units.reusable_pattern: We hand annotated [a public source], and manually entered [the fields] to create [the structure].
reusable_elements: occurrences: page 4, section 3.1.
stable function: make a homemade graph auditable instead of pretending it was downloaded.
pattern: hand annotated X and manually entered Y.
boundary: say which fields were typed; do not hide the manual step.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not treat a hand graph as survey-grade geometry.

units.function: reduce an unimpeded travel time to one sentence a reader can check

original_instantiations: At the simplest level, the longest anyone takes to get out, if nobody is in the way, is just the longest of the shortest routes from each room to a door.
Ignoring crowds, the worst exit time is simply the maximum, over rooms, of the shortest path to a door.

units.source_excerpt: At the most basic level, we can analyze the graph as follows: considering only the estimated time to travel from one room to another, the maximum time for an unimpeded museum-goer to exit the building is simply the maximum time over the shortest paths to the exit from each room.
units.reusable_pattern: At the most basic level, [ignoring interaction], [the worst case] is simply [a max over shortest paths].
reusable_elements: occurrences: page 4, section 3.2.
stable function: give a closed-form baseline before congestion is added.
pattern: is simply the maximum over the shortest paths.
boundary: the sentence must name what it ignores, or it overclaims.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not report this time as the evacuation time once crowding is in the model.

units.function: reject a shortest-path recommendation by naming the congestion it walks through

original_instantiations: Note that responders would be told to take the same corridor the crowd is using, only backward. That is unrealistic, since the short route may run through rooms that are already packed.
The short path for a responder is the crowd's path in reverse. That recommendation fails once those rooms are full.

units.source_excerpt: Note that in this case, security personnel would be recommended to take the same path as bystanders moving in the opposite direction. This situation is unrealistic since the shortest path to a target location may pass through heavily congested rooms.
units.reusable_pattern: Note that [the naive advice]. This situation is unrealistic since [the path may pass through the crowded place].
reusable_elements: occurrences: page 4, section 3.2, second paragraph.
stable function: kill a graph-distance policy before the next model is introduced.
pattern: would be recommended to X. This is unrealistic since Y.
boundary: Y must be a mechanism the later model actually represents.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not claim shortest paths are never useful for responders.

units.function: abandon an exact but intractable constant and report a bound

features.quantitative_role: replaces an exact value with an interval
original_instantiations: Solving for the exact cut is far too expensive, so we bound the constant instead and report the interval the theorem gives.
The exact quantity is too costly to compute, therefore we keep the inequality and quote the range.

units.source_excerpt: This is very computationally complex to solve, therefore we bound this constant instead.
units.reusable_pattern: This is very computationally complex to solve, therefore we bound [the constant] instead.
reusable_elements: occurrences: page 5, section 3.3.
stable function: tell the reader why a number is an interval.
pattern: too complex, therefore we bound it instead.
boundary: the bound must be cited and numerically evaluated, not waved at.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not present the midpoint of a wide Cheeger interval as a measured bottleneck.

units.function: read a small spectral gap as evidence the graph splits on a thin cut

original_instantiations: Notice that in the worst case the number is tiny. That means the network can be split in two by cutting only a few links.
Look at the lower end: it is very small, which says the layout falls into two pieces across a thin cut.

units.source_excerpt: Notice that in the worst case this value is very small. This indicates that our graph can be broken into two pieces with only a small cut.
units.reusable_pattern: Notice that in the worst case [the number] is very small. This indicates that [the structure] can be broken with only [a small cut].
reusable_elements: occurrences: page 5, section 3.3, closing sentences.
stable function: convert a spectral number into a floor-plan claim.
pattern: Notice that in the worst case. This indicates.
boundary: say it is the worst case of a bound, not a counted cut, until the partition is drawn.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not treat a Cheeger lower bound as the number of doors that fail.

units.function: drop from a picture to the count of links the cut actually severs

original_instantiations: Looking harder at the split, we find it cuts only a handful of corridors, and one of them is an entrance itself.
Once we inspect the partition, only a few links are cut, and one of those links is a main door.

units.source_excerpt: Diving into the data, we find that the partition severs only 4 corridors.
units.reusable_pattern: Diving into the data, we find that [the picture] severs only [a small count] of [links].
reusable_elements: occurrences: page 7, section 3.4.
stable function: cash a spectral drawing into a corridor count.
pattern: Diving into the data, we find that only N.
boundary: N must be checkable on the figure.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not use the phrase to introduce a result that is not a count from the figure just shown.

units.function: state a data hole, then say what assumption fills it

original_instantiations: Some emergency doors are not on any public plan. Assuming the designer wanted a short trip to a door, we put candidate doors where the average distance is smallest.
A few exits are withheld from the public drawings. If the designer cared about short egress, those doors should sit where mean distance to an exit is lowest.

units.source_excerpt: A number of emergency exits from the Louvre are kept from public knowledge; they are not on any publicly available floor plan. Only the emergency personnel and museum staff known the locations of these exits. However, assuming that the designer of the building desired efficient egress in the event of an emergency, we can expect exits to be placed in locations that minimize the average path length to an exit.
units.reusable_pattern: [Objects] are kept from public knowledge. However, assuming [the designer wanted X], we can expect them where [X is minimized].
reusable_elements: occurrences: page 7, section 3.5.
stable function: replace a missing coordinate with an explicit design hypothesis.
pattern: kept from public knowledge. However, assuming the designer desired.
boundary: label the placements as guesses; do not write them as observed exits.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not claim hidden exits were located, only that candidates were proposed.

units.function: list what the current model cannot see, then point at the next model

original_instantiations: This network view misses two plain facts: a room fills up, and it cannot tell a jam from a security risk. The next model takes those on.
The algebraic picture does not see capacity, and it flags risks rather than jams. We pick those up in the model that follows.

units.source_excerpt: This an algebraic graph theoretic model does not consider a number of salient realities that afflict the Louvre. We address these issues with the subsequent model.
units.reusable_pattern: This [model] does not consider [the realities]. We address these issues with the subsequent model.
reusable_elements: occurrences: page 7, section 3.6.
stable function: make a limitation the reason the next model exists.
pattern: does not consider. We address these with the subsequent model.
boundary: every listed gap must be handled, or named as still open, later.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not use the handoff sentence if the next section does not treat the listed gaps.

units.function: reopen a section by pointing back at the limitation just named

original_instantiations: As we said, the first model is useful and still blind to how people get in each other's way. Here we add the crowd acting on itself.
The connectivity picture helps, and it still leaves out self-interaction. This section puts that back in.

units.source_excerpt: Like we mentioned, while the connectivity model gives us useful insights, it doesn't take into consideration many other factors at play. In this section, we formulate a model that takes into account both connectivity, structure and crowd self-interaction.
units.reusable_pattern: Like we mentioned, while [the previous model] gives useful insights, it doesn't take into consideration [the missing factor]. In this section we take into account [both].
reusable_elements: occurrences: page 7, opening of section 4.
stable function: start a new model without pretending the old one was useless.
pattern: while X gives insights, it doesn't take into consideration Y.
boundary: spoken register is part of the move; do not polish it into 'notwithstanding'.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not open every section this way; it belongs after a shortcomings list.

units.function: postpone a scenario so the base model can be explained cleanly

original_instantiations: So the base case stays readable, we leave the damaged-building cases out for now and point to the later section.
To explain the plain model first, adaptable cases wait. They are in the sensitivity section.

units.source_excerpt: For the purpose of explaining the model effectively, we do not yet include discussion on adaptable scenarios. For information on adaptable scenarios, refer to Section 6.
units.reusable_pattern: For the purpose of explaining [the model] effectively, we do not yet include [the variant]. Refer to [the later section].
reusable_elements: occurrences: page 7, section 4 opener.
stable function: keep a base-case explanation from being read as the whole study.
pattern: we do not yet include X. Refer to Section N.
boundary: the later section must exist and must treat X.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not defer a result the decision actually depends on without returning to it.

units.function: turn two public numbers into the population the simulation will use

features.quantitative_role: derives a stock from a flow and a dwell time
original_instantiations: Public figures put arrivals near a few thousand an hour. We take a typical visit as lasting a few hours, and so the building holds on the order of several thousand people at once.
From an hourly arrival rate and a guessed length of visit, we get the number of people inside during opening hours.

units.source_excerpt: The number of people entering the Louvre is on average 2,532.83 people/hr for 2017. We estimate that on average a museum-goer will spend 3 hrs in the Louvre. Thus, we calculate that the average population in the Louvre during opening hours is 7,598.49 people.
units.reusable_pattern: [A public rate] is [number]. We estimate that [a dwell time]. Thus, we calculate that [the stock] is [number].
reusable_elements: occurrences: page 8, section 4.2.
stable function: show a Little's-law step without naming the theorem.
pattern: on average X. We estimate Y. Thus we calculate Z.
boundary: mark which input is estimated and which is cited.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not quote the product to two decimals as if both inputs were measured.

units.function: import a distribution by naming the theorem and the citation in one clause

original_instantiations: Queueing theory says that if k events are spread uniformly in time, the gap between them follows an Erlang law, so that is the transfer time we draw.
A standard queueing result gives an Erlang gap when k events sit uniformly in time, and we use that for the time to move k people.

units.source_excerpt: From queuing theory we know that given k events uniformly distributed in time, the time between events follows an Erlang distribution.
units.reusable_pattern: From [a named theory] we know that given [a condition], [the quantity] follows [a distribution].
reusable_elements: occurrences: page 8, section 4.3.
stable function: attach a distribution to a citation instead of inventing one.
pattern: From X we know that given Y, Z follows D.
boundary: the condition (uniform events) must match how the simulation samples.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not cite Erlang and then sample something else without saying the reduction.

units.function: break a constant parameter because the assumption just stated forbids it

original_instantiations: The mean time per move will not stay fixed. It grows as the jam builds, so the rate is a base rate scaled by how full the room already is.
Mean transfer time is not a constant. Once people block each other, the rate has to depend on how crowded the room of origin is.

units.source_excerpt: However, given the assumption of crowd self-interaction, the average time per transfer, 1/mu, will not be constant. Indeed, the average time increases as congestion forms.
units.reusable_pattern: However, given [the assumption], [the parameter] will not be constant. Indeed, it increases as [the jam] forms.
reusable_elements: occurrences: page 8, section 4.3.
stable function: justify a state-dependent rate in prose before the formula.
pattern: will not be constant. Indeed, it increases as.
boundary: the formula that follows must implement the increase, not a decrease.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not claim every service rate in a crowd model must be exponential in density.

units.function: restate a penalty constant in ordinary motion language

original_instantiations: Put plainly, the more people already in the room you are leaving, the harder it is to step into the next one.
In short, a fuller starting room makes the move to the next room slower.

units.source_excerpt: In other words, the more people in the starting room, the harder it becomes to move to the other room.
units.reusable_pattern: In other words, the more [state], the harder it becomes to [the action].
reusable_elements: occurrences: page 9, section 4.3.
stable function: give a judge the sentence under the formula.
pattern: In other words, the more X, the harder Y.
boundary: the gloss must match the sign of the formula.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not add a mechanism in the gloss that the equation does not have.

units.function: narrate a discrete-event loop in the order the code would run

original_instantiations: For each link that still has someone to move, we draw an exponential wait. Time jumps to the soonest wait. If that person is not blocked we move them and shrink every other wait; if they are blocked we add another draw and try the next.
We schedule one person per busy link with a random wait, advance to the earliest, move them if the room has space, and otherwise push their clock and look again.

units.source_excerpt: To move time forward we find the edge with the soonest time. If we can we, move that person and they are not blocked, then we advance time by that amount and transfer them to the room they were going to. If not, we add another random number to their time and try the next soonest event.
units.reusable_pattern: To move time forward we find [the soonest event]. If we can, we [apply it]. If not, we [postpone it] and try the next.
reusable_elements: occurrences: page 9, after Algorithm 2.
stable function: let a reader simulate one step without reading the pseudocode.
pattern: If we can we, move. If not, add another random number.
boundary: keep the spoken slip only if the success and failure branches are both clear.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not treat this narration as a convergence proof.

units.function: say why an existing simulator can absorb a second kind of agent

original_instantiations: The same simulator is a good place to put the responders. They follow the visitors' rules, except they get to move first.
An agent model is a natural home for the rescue teams: same interactions, but they have priority.

units.source_excerpt: The agent-based model provides an excellent paradigm to simulate the behavior emergency response personnel. Indeed, the emergency personnel follow the same behaviors and interactions as normal evacuees, but have priority in movement over others.
units.reusable_pattern: [The existing model] provides an excellent paradigm to simulate [a second actor]. Indeed, they follow the same [rules], but [one difference].
reusable_elements: occurrences: page 9, section 4.4.
stable function: add an agent class without a new model section.
pattern: excellent paradigm. Indeed, same behaviors, but priority.
boundary: name the one difference or the reuse is empty.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not say two agent classes are the same when more than one rule differs.

units.function: state a prediction before showing the figure that tests it

original_instantiations: We guessed that arriving in the middle of the evacuation would be slowest, because that is when the jam peaks.
Our bet was that a mid-evacuation arrival hits the worst crowding, so the trip takes longest then.

units.source_excerpt: We guessed that seeking the target area in the middle of the evacuation will take the longest because that is when peak congestion occurs.
units.reusable_pattern: We guessed that [an action] at [a time] will take the longest because [the mechanism peaks then].
reusable_elements: occurrences: page 10, before Figure 5.
stable function: put a falsifiable sentence in front of a bar chart.
pattern: We guessed that X because Y.
boundary: the next paragraph must say whether the figure agreed.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not upgrade a guess to a finding if the figure is only descriptive.

units.function: pull one timing claim out of a crowded bar chart

features.quantitative_role: reads a peak off a chart
original_instantiations: One thing the chart shows is when the jam looks worst at each density. At a low density the slow arrival sits near five minutes; at a higher density it sits nearer ten.
The bars tell us the crowded moment shifts later as the building gets fuller.

units.source_excerpt: An interesting insight from this is that we can glean when congestion seems to be highest for each density. For example, for a museum population density of 0.3, congestion seems to be highest around 5 minutes.
units.reusable_pattern: An interesting insight from this is that we can glean [when the bad case happens]. For example, at [setting], it seems highest around [time].
reusable_elements: occurrences: page 10, after Figure 5.
stable function: convert a grouped bar chart into a when-claim.
pattern: an interesting insight is that we can glean. For example.
boundary: hedge with seems when the chart was averaged and not tested.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not report a visual peak as a statistically identified change point.

units.function: offer a counterintuitive action only in the regime where the chart supports it

original_instantiations: Going in at once is best across the densities we tried. From the same chart, waiting can be the smarter move when the threat is mild and the building is not full.
Immediate entry wins in general. At low density, a deliberate delay can still be reasonable if the threat is not urgent.

units.source_excerpt: From this graph, we can also see that it may be strategic for the emergency personnel to delay their appearance when the threat is not critical – typically with lower densities.
units.reusable_pattern: From this graph, it may be strategic to [delay] when [the threat is not critical] – typically at [the low setting].
reusable_elements: occurrences: page 10, section 4.4.
stable function: let a figure authorize an exception without overturning the main advice.
pattern: it may be strategic to X when Y – typically with Z.
boundary: keep may; the paper did not optimize the delay.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not recommend delaying rescue as a general policy.

units.function: introduce an aggregate model with a physical analogy and a hedge

original_instantiations: A crowd moving through the rooms can be treated, in bulk, as something like a thick fluid seeping through a porous block.
Taken together, the people behave a bit like a fluid whose thickness rises when they are packed, moving through a porous layout.

units.source_excerpt: Crowds traveling through the Louvre during an evacuation could be modeled in aggregate as something similar to a viscous non-Newtonian fluid percolating through a porous substrate.
units.reusable_pattern: [The crowd] could be modeled in aggregate as something similar to [a physical system].
reusable_elements: occurrences: page 11, section 5 opener.
stable function: license a continuum equation without claiming people are a fluid.
pattern: could be modeled in aggregate as something similar to.
boundary: keep could and something similar to; the analogy is not an identity.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not import fluid theorems that the paper never uses.

units.function: disarm a technical word that has an everyday meaning in this setting

original_instantiations: A reader might think we mean people under strain. Here the word means force per area, the mechanical kind.
The everyday reading is emotional strain. We mean the mechanical quantity, force over area.

units.source_excerpt: One would imagine that museum-goers are stressed when evacuation but here we mean the force over area kind.
units.reusable_pattern: One would imagine that [the everyday reading], but here we mean [the technical reading].
reusable_elements: occurrences: page 11, footnote under section 5.1.
stable function: keep a metaphor from being read as a psychological claim.
pattern: One would imagine X but here we mean Y.
boundary: only when the same word carries both meanings in the paragraph.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not use the footnote to smuggle in a stress model the equations do not have.

units.function: tie a new term to the mechanism already simulated

original_instantiations: The blocking term matters because nothing can flow into a room that is already full. It does the same job as rescheduling a transfer when the destination has no space.
A full room accepts no inflow. That term plays the role the simulator's blocked events already played.

units.source_excerpt: The effect of this term on the behavior of the system is analogous to the way transfer events in the agent-based model are rescheduled when they are blocked.
units.reusable_pattern: The effect of [this term] is analogous to the way [the earlier model] handles [the same event].
reusable_elements: occurrences: page 12, section 5.2.
stable function: show two models are the same idea at two scales.
pattern: is analogous to the way X are rescheduled when Y.
boundary: the analogy must name the shared event, not just say the models agree.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not claim numerical agreement from an analogy sentence.

units.function: discard a degenerate damage case before spending words on the connected one

original_instantiations: The dull case is total cutoff: nobody can leave, and the clock then depends on ladders and repairs. The case worth modeling is damage that still leaves some path out.
If damage seals the building, exit time is no longer a routing question. We keep the cases where the plan stays connected.

units.source_excerpt: The most trivial case is when some damage completely disallows visitors to exit the building. A more relevant situation occurs when disconnections still keep our floor plan a connected graph.
units.reusable_pattern: The most trivial case is when [the problem disappears]. A more relevant situation occurs when [the structure still works, but barely].
reusable_elements: occurrences: page 13, section 6.1.
stable function: show the scope cut instead of hiding it.
pattern: most trivial case. A more relevant situation.
boundary: say what makes the discarded case trivial.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not call a case trivial merely because it is hard.

units.function: bring in a lopsided crowd with a hedged popular claim plus a picture

original_instantiations: People say most visitors come for one famous object. A map of tagged photos from one year does pile up in that room, so a fairer test puts more people there and thins the rest.
A common claim is that one room draws the bulk of the crowd. The photo map agrees, so we shift density toward the famous rooms and hold the total fixed.

units.source_excerpt: It's been said that something like 80% of people go to the Louvre just to see the Mona Lisa. Indeed, a visualization tracking Geo-tagged Instagram photos in 2014 shows the area nearby has a significant higher density of people.
units.reusable_pattern: It's been said that [a lopsided fact]. Indeed, [an independent picture] shows [the same pile-up].
reusable_elements: occurrences: page 14, section 6.2.
stable function: justify a nonuniform initial condition without a census.
pattern: It's been said. Indeed, a visualization shows.
boundary: the folk number stays hedged; the photo map is the evidence.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not treat a magazine percentage as a measured room count.

units.function: say a monotone result matches the expectation, then add the factor that did not matter

original_instantiations: As the plot shows, a fuller building takes longer to clear, which matches the hunch that more people and more bumping both cost time. More doors shorten it. Shifting people toward the famous rooms, though, barely changes the total.
Clearance time rises with density, as expected, and falls as doors are added. Where the people start matters much less than how many there are.

units.source_excerpt: As we see from Figure 9, as the density increases, so does the time to fully evacuate. This is consistent with our intuition that higher densities require more people to move out of the building and that there are things like crowd-interaction at play. However, we don't see a significant difference when the distribution of persons is not uniform.
units.reusable_pattern: As we see from [the figure], as [X] increases, so does [Y]. This is consistent with our intuition. However, we don't see a significant difference when [Z].
reusable_elements: occurrences: page 15, section 6.3.
stable function: pair a confirming trend with the factor that dropped out.
pattern: consistent with our intuition. However, we don't see a significant difference.
boundary: significant here is visual, not a reported test; do not add a p-value.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not generalize the null result beyond the distributions the simulation tried.

units.function: offer a mechanism for a sharp worsening without claiming it was isolated

original_instantiations: Cut links make exit time jump once the building is full. The slowdown and the time spent turning signs around appear to stack.
At high density a severed link hurts far more. Crowd friction and the delay of reversing the signs look like they compound.

units.source_excerpt: It seems that crowd self-interaction with higher penalties combined with the time required to effectively reverse exit sign direction has a compounding effect in higher densities.
units.reusable_pattern: It seems that [mechanism A] combined with [mechanism B] has a compounding effect at [the high setting].
reusable_elements: occurrences: page 15, section 6.3.
stable function: name an interaction the design did not factorialize.
pattern: it seems that A combined with B has a compounding effect.
boundary: keep it seems; the paper did not separate the two causes.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not write the compounding as an estimated interaction coefficient.

units.function: turn a null sensitivity into permission to skip a data collection

original_instantiations: So it is fair to judge an exit plan without a head count per room, and to spread people evenly instead.
Because the starting pattern barely moved the answer, a uniform spread is enough for comparing plans.

units.source_excerpt: Therefore, it is reasonable to evaluate exit strategies without gathering the population per room statistic and instead using a uniform distribution of persons.
units.reusable_pattern: Therefore, it is reasonable to evaluate [the decision] without gathering [the fine data] and instead using [the simple substitute].
reusable_elements: occurrences: page 15, section 6.3.
stable function: convert insensitivity into a data recommendation.
pattern: it is reasonable to evaluate without gathering X and instead using Y.
boundary: only after the sensitivity that justifies the skip.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not drop room-level data for a question the paper found was sensitive, such as which corridor is cut.

units.function: deny a model one job and assign it another in the next sentence

original_instantiations: This model will not give you a clearance time. What it does give is a structural reading of which links an exit plan depends on.
It is the wrong tool for a clock time. It is the right tool for asking which corridors the plan cannot afford to lose.

units.source_excerpt: This model is not effective at determining the evacuation time for a given plan. However, the analysis done on this model yielded some very key insights into the structure.
units.reusable_pattern: This model is not effective at [job A]. However, it yielded [job B].
reusable_elements: occurrences: page 16, section 7.1.
stable function: stop a comparison section from ranking models on one axis.
pattern: not effective at A. However, key insights into B.
boundary: both jobs must be ones the paper actually attempted.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not rank the three models as a single winner.

units.function: tie expected accuracy to the unit the model respects

original_instantiations: Because the model is built on queues, we expect it to track people who really are separate bodies moving room to room.
The theory matches the thing being counted, discrete visitors, so we expect the trajectories to be the believable ones.

units.source_excerpt: This model is based on queuing theory and so we expect it to accurately model how visitors (which are discrete entities) move through the museum.
units.reusable_pattern: This model is based on [a theory] and so we expect it to accurately model [the unit that theory respects].
reusable_elements: occurrences: page 16, section 7.2.
stable function: give the reason one model is trusted for individuals.
pattern: based on X and so we expect it to accurately model Y.
boundary: expectation is not a validation result.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not treat a matching unit as empirical accuracy.

units.function: assign a deterministic model the role of an average, and admit it would not tune

original_instantiations: Being deterministic, this version is best read as a picture of average behavior. We also found it stubborn to tune, which stopped us going further.
The continuum version stands in for a mean path. It resisted calibration, so the deeper analysis never happened.

units.source_excerpt: This model is also deterministic and so could best be understood as a model of average behavior. However, we also found this model to be very hard to tune which prevented in depth analysis.
units.reusable_pattern: [The model] is deterministic and so could best be understood as [an average]. However, we found it very hard to tune, which prevented [the deeper pass].
reusable_elements: occurrences: page 16-17, section 7.3.
stable function: report a model that was built and then not used much.
pattern: could best be understood as. However, hard to tune, which prevented.
boundary: do not hide the failed tuning behind the analogy.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not present the differential model as jointly validated with the agent model.

units.function: point a future experiment at a policy the current runs did not test

original_instantiations: So far the continuum runs start everyone spread evenly. Changing that start could say whether splitting large tour groups would shorten the exit.
The quick model has only seen a flat initial crowd. A different start might argue for a rule that breaks up big groups.

units.source_excerpt: Currently, our analysis for this model only investigated situations with uniform density initial conditions. Altering the initial conditions could give further insight. This might suggest a museum policy of breaking up large groups of tourists.
units.reusable_pattern: Currently we only investigated [one condition]. Altering it could give further insight. This might suggest a policy of [an action].
reusable_elements: occurrences: page 17, section 8.1.
stable function: keep a policy idea in the future-work tense.
pattern: currently only X. Altering could. This might suggest.
boundary: might stays; the sentence is unfinished in the source and must not be completed as a result.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not recommend breaking up groups as a finding of this paper.

units.function: admit an analysis was not done and still name the question it would have answered

original_instantiations: We did not get far with the continuum model, but a correlation of room densities over time could show whether one jam drags another along.
Little was done with the differential version. It could still say whether congestion in two rooms rises together, which would tell us how to aim the signs to break that link.

units.source_excerpt: While we were unable to do much analysis on the differential flow model, but it has the potential to give key insights into how congestion forms.
units.reusable_pattern: While we were unable to do much analysis on [the model], it has the potential to give key insights into [the question].
reusable_elements: occurrences: page 17, section 8.3.
stable function: leave a tool on the table without pretending it was used.
pattern: unable to do much, but it has the potential.
boundary: the insight stays potential.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not cite cross-correlation results this paper did not compute.

units.function: state the decision exception the bottleneck metric exists to catch

original_instantiations: Pointing every sign at the nearest door is a strong first rule. Our jam measures say there are cases where a longer route thins the crowd and, oddly, gets people out sooner.
Nearest door is a good default. Sometimes a longer path cuts the jam enough to clear the building faster, which is the opposite of the guess.

units.source_excerpt: However, our methods of identifying bottlenecks indicate that there are situations where a longer path might actually reduce congestion and hence counter-intuitively speed up egress.
units.reusable_pattern: However, [the metric] indicates there are situations where [a worse local choice] might actually [help] and hence counter-intuitively [improve the global time].
reusable_elements: occurrences: page 17, section 9.
stable function: keep the headline recommendation from being the heuristic it started as.
pattern: a longer path might actually reduce congestion and hence counter-intuitively speed up.
boundary: might; the paper proposes an optimizer, it does not exhibit the improved signing.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not claim a longer path was shown to be faster for a named corridor.

units.function: hand the search procedure to the client instead of pretending it was already run

features.clause_structure: using our model we would suggest
original_instantiations: With the agent simulator in hand, we would hand the signing problem to a genetic search or to simulated annealing, and ask whether the nearest-door rule needs a correction.
We would not claim the signs are optimal. We would run a search on the simulator to see whether nearest-door should be edited.

units.source_excerpt: Using our agent-based model, we would suggest using a genetic algorithm or simulated annealing optimization scheme to determine whether or not a closest exit strategy needs modification.
units.reusable_pattern: Using [our model], we would suggest using [a search method] to determine whether or not [the heuristic] needs modification.
reusable_elements: occurrences: page 17, section 9.
stable function: recommend a computation rather than fake its output.
pattern: we would suggest using an optimizer to determine whether or not.
boundary: whether or not must stay; the paper did not run the search.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not report an optimized sign plan this paper does not contain.

units.function: tell the decision maker to use the model as an instrument with a bound

features.quantitative_role: sets an upper bound as the decision criterion
original_instantiations: The simulator can time any number of doors in any places, so we advise the managers to use it to pick a number of doors that keeps clearance time under a ceiling they choose.
Because the model scores any exit set, the leaders should use it to choose how many doors to open so that exit time stays under a bound.

units.source_excerpt: Since the simulation can determine time to exit for any number of exits at different locations, we advise the museum leaders to utilize it to determine the number of exits such that the evacuation time has an upper bound.
units.reusable_pattern: Since [the model] can determine [the outcome] for any [choice], we advise [the client] to utilize it to determine [the choice] such that [the outcome] has an upper bound.
reusable_elements: occurrences: page 18, section 9.
stable function: deliver a procedure and a criterion, not a single number.
pattern: we advise the leaders to utilize it to determine N such that T has an upper bound.
boundary: the bound is theirs to set; the paper does not name its value.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not invent the number of exits the museum should open.

units.function: record that the bibliography mixes theorem, data, journalism and a how-to

original_instantiations: The reference list puts a graph-theory note next to a visitor-count table, a newspaper piece, a photo essay and a room-capacity how-to.
Citations run from a Cheeger inequality to a statistics portal, a news article and a tour advertisement.

units.source_excerpt: F. R. K Chung. Laplacians of graphs and Cheeger inequalities. Louvre Museum. Number of Visitors. C. Vogel. On a Mission to Loosen Up the Louvre. The New York Times.
units.reusable_pattern: The list cites [a theorem], [an official count], [journalism] and [a practical how-to] side by side.
reusable_elements: occurrences: page 19, references.
stable function: show the authority mix a policy paper actually used.
boundary: paper-specific list; not a template for what to cite.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not treat a newspaper percentage as equal in weight to the visitor series.
